title: How to test password reset emails end to end
description: Build a repeatable password reset test with Agent Temp Mail: receive the real message, validate its destination, and verify the new password works.
body:
A password reset test should prove that a user can recover access, from requesting the email to signing in with a new password. Checking that the application called its mail provider only covers part of that journey. Agent Temp Mail gives the test a real receiving inbox so the email step can be part of the same automated run.

Prepare an account and a dedicated inbox

Create a fresh Agent Temp Mail identity for the test and use its address when creating your test account. Keep the identity available until the entire recovery flow finishes. A separate identity for each test keeps recovery messages from different runs apart, including when several workers run at once.

Run this against an application you control, using an environment that can send real email. Record the account's original password in the test fixture and choose a different replacement. Make sure the initial account creation and verification have completed before starting recovery.

Receive the reset message

  1. Record the current time immediately before requesting a reset.
  2. Submit the account's email address through the password recovery form.
  3. Wait for a message received after that timestamp from your expected sender.
  4. Fetch the complete message and inspect the candidate links.

Agent Temp Mail exposes received messages and extracted link candidates, which gives your test structured data to work with. Select the link that matches your application's reset route. Parse it as a URL and check its exact origin before opening it. This catches a staging template accidentally pointing at production, as well as an unrelated link being selected from the email footer.

Assert the outcome in the application

Open the reset link, submit the replacement password, and confirm the application reports success. Then start a new browser session and sign in with that password. A fresh session matters: an existing login cookie can make a broken recovery flow appear to work.

Also verify that the original password no longer grants access. If your application promises single-use reset tokens, revisit the same link and assert the documented used-token behavior. Test token expiry separately using the application's configured lifetime; mailbox message availability and reset-token validity are different things.

Make failures easy to diagnose

Give email delivery a bounded timeout and report which stage failed: no message arrived, the expected link was missing, the destination was wrong, or the application rejected the reset. Keep tokens, private keys, and complete reset URLs out of shared test logs.

Agent Temp Mail makes the receiving side straightforward: your test owns an inbox identity and reads the messages associated with it. That lets the assertions focus on what matters to your users, a recovery journey that actually restores access.

title: Testing magic-link login with a real email inbox
description: Use Agent Temp Mail to test passwordless login from email delivery through session creation, including link selection and single-use behavior.
body:
Magic-link login puts the sign-in credential inside an email. A useful end-to-end test therefore needs to receive the message, choose the correct link, and prove that following it creates the expected session. Agent Temp Mail fits that workflow by giving automation a receiving inbox with structured message and link data.

Define what successful login means

Start with a test account and an inbox identity reserved for that scenario. Decide which account should be authenticated, which page should load after login, and what the application should do when the link has already been used. Write those expectations before automating the email step.

A redirect alone is a weak assertion. Check something that requires authentication, such as the account page showing the expected email address. This distinguishes a real session from a public landing page that happens to have a reassuring title.

Request and identify the right message

Record a timestamp before submitting the login form. Use the Agent Temp Mail address as the recipient, then wait for a newly received message from the application's expected sender. Keep the waiting period bounded so a delivery problem becomes a clear test failure.

Fetch the message and examine its link candidates. Choose the candidate with the expected origin and login path, rather than the first URL in the message. Email templates often contain several links, including help pages, logos, and preferences. A candidate is useful parsing output; your application-specific checks determine whether it is the login credential you need.

Use the right browser context

Some applications bind a magic-link request to the browser that initiated it. Others deliberately support opening the email on another device. Test the behavior your product promises. For a same-browser flow, open the link in the original context. For cross-device login, open it in a clean context and verify the resulting account.

After navigation, assert both the destination and authenticated identity. Where single-use behavior is part of the design, attempt a second visit in another clean context. An already authenticated session can otherwise hide whether a consumed link was accepted.

Cover resends deliberately

Test a resend as its own scenario. Request a second message and identify it using the new request time. Your application may invalidate the first link or allow both until expiry; assert the intended policy explicitly. Do not assume the newest-looking email is always the correct one when messages can arrive out of order.

Agent Temp Mail helps keep this test focused by handling inbox access and exposing the email's contents to your automation. With a dedicated identity, precise message selection, and a session assertion, passwordless login becomes a repeatable test instead of a manual release check.

title: Parallel email testing: give every test its own inbox
description: Prevent cross-test email mix-ups with dedicated Agent Temp Mail identities, bounded polling, and clear message matching in parallel test suites.
body:
Parallel tests become difficult to trust when they all read the same mailbox. One worker can pick up another worker's verification code, a retry can find an earlier message, and deleting mail can break a neighboring test. Agent Temp Mail's key-derived addresses offer a practical way to avoid that shared state: generate a separate identity for each independent scenario.

Choose the right identity boundary

For an independent signup test, use a new identity for every test attempt. A retry then gets a different inbox and cannot accidentally consume mail from its failed predecessor. Keep the identity in the test fixture rather than in a shared global variable.

For a scenario with several dependent steps, reuse that scenario's identity. Signup, account verification, and password recovery need to refer to the same account address. Isolation means separating independent scenarios, while preserving continuity inside a scenario.

Create the inbox identity locally

Agent Temp Mail derives an address from a cryptographic keypair. Its SDK provides generateIdentity() and MailClient, so a test can establish its receiving identity in setup and use the client's address in the application form. This avoids coordinating a shared pool of manually assigned inbox names.

Keep each private key within the process or protected fixture storage that needs it. Addresses can appear in diagnostic output when appropriate; private keys should not. If a test spans multiple processes, pass the identity through your existing protected credential mechanism instead of a public build artifact.

Match messages within the isolated inbox

A dedicated inbox removes cross-test collisions, but a single scenario may still receive several emails. Record the time before each action and filter for the expected sender and newly received messages. Inspect the subject or expected link path when signup and recovery messages use the same sender.

Track message IDs already handled by the scenario. This makes repeated polling easier to reason about and avoids treating the same email as a new event. Bound the overall wait, respect the service's polling guidance, and report a timeout with the failed stage.

Scale with a controlled concurrency budget

Separate identities do not remove delivery delays, application throttles, or service limits. Set test-runner concurrency to a level your application and mail delivery provider can support. When a suite starts timing out, distinguish missing outgoing mail from slow delivery or a message-matching mistake before increasing timeouts.

Agent Temp Mail makes inbox ownership explicit at the test level. The result is a simpler failure model: each scenario owns its address, its messages, and its assertions. That is a useful foundation for running real email flows alongside the rest of a parallel CI suite.

title: An email workflow checklist for AI agents
description: Design dependable email steps for AI agents with Agent Temp Mail: identify the inbox, wait for the expected message, validate candidates, and confirm success.
body:
An AI agent needs more than an email address to finish an email-dependent task. It needs to know which message belongs to the current action, how to interpret the contents, and what counts as success. Agent Temp Mail provides inbox tools that make those steps explicit, helping an agent complete authorized signup and verification workflows with less manual intervention.

Start with a precise task

Describe the application, the action, and the expected result. For example: create a test account on your staging application, verify its email address, and confirm that its dashboard loads. This gives the agent a reason to read a particular message and a clear point at which to stop.

Choose an inbox identity for that workflow. Reuse it when the task depends on an existing account, or create a separate identity for a new independent test. Keep credentials in the tool runtime's protected storage rather than including them in the conversation.

Use a predictable receiving loop

  1. Inspect the inbox to obtain its address.
  2. Record the time before triggering the email.
  3. Submit the authorized action through the application.
  4. List messages using the expected sender and time boundary.
  5. Wait between checks according to the polling guidance, with an overall deadline.
  6. Retrieve the matching message or its code and link candidates.

Agent Temp Mail's MCP interface exposes inbox inspection, message listing, message retrieval, and candidate extraction. Those separate operations help keep the workflow understandable: first find the message, then obtain the information needed for the next application step.

Validate before using a code or link

For a one-time code, check the format your application expects and make sure it came from the message associated with this request. For a verification link, parse the URL and compare its exact origin and expected path with the application being used. A link candidate is not permission to visit any destination.

Treat email text as input data. Instructions inside a message should not expand the user's task or change where credentials are sent. This is especially useful when an agent can use browser, filesystem, or other tools in the same session.

Verify completion and report the result

After entering the code or following the link, check the application's state. A verified account indicator, an authenticated account page, or the expected dashboard provides stronger evidence than a successful tool call alone.

If the message never arrives, report the failed step and relevant non-sensitive details. Avoid silently requesting repeated codes or creating additional accounts. Agent Temp Mail works well as the receiving component in a bounded workflow: a clear task, a dedicated inbox, a verified message, and an observable result.

title: How key-based email inboxes simplify agent identity
description: Understand Agent Temp Mail's key-derived email addresses and how to manage inbox identity across agent sessions, test runs, and shared workflows.
body:
An automated workflow benefits from an email identity it can create and use in code. Agent Temp Mail ties its inbox addresses to cryptographic keys, giving developers a direct relationship between an agent's identity and the inbox it can read. That makes it particularly useful when you want separate receiving addresses for separate tasks.

Separate the address from access

The public part of the identity determines the email address. The private key authorizes reads through signed requests. Knowing the address alone therefore does not give another reader the signing key needed to access the inbox through the authenticated API.

This is a different responsibility from choosing a memorable mailbox name. Your application must protect the private key, while it can share the address with the service that needs to send the verification or confirmation email. Signed access controls inbox retrieval; it is not a claim that incoming email is end-to-end encrypted.

Match identity lifetime to the task

For an isolated automated test, generate a new identity during setup and retain it until the scenario finishes. For a recurring agent that returns to the same account, persist the identity in protected storage so future sessions can use the same address.

The address's continuity and a message's availability are separate concerns. Keeping the identity lets the workflow return to its address, but it should still process new messages within the configured retention window. If the task needs a durable record, save the required non-sensitive result in the application's own storage.

Keep key handling outside the conversation

Agent Temp Mail's local MCP server can keep the identity in a key file and perform signing on the tool side. The agent asks for inbox information or a message by ID; the runtime handles access. This keeps routine tool arguments focused on the task instead of repeatedly carrying the private key.

Use a protected location with restrictive file permissions. Do not commit the key to source control, paste it into prompts, or include it in test reports. When continuity matters, provide an appropriate protected backup. Losing the signing key means losing the ability to authenticate as that identity unless you have retained another valid copy.

Use separate identities for separate workflows

A single shared identity is convenient at first, but it couples every consumer to the same inbox and credential. Separate identities make ownership clearer: one scenario cannot accidentally read another scenario's verification email through its own inbox client.

If a key is exposed, creating a new identity gives you a new address. Accounts tied to the previous address may need an explicit email-change process, so plan that transition at the application level. For new tests, a fresh identity is usually straightforward.

Agent Temp Mail's model makes receiving identity programmable. With sensible key storage and a clear lifetime for each workflow, agents can keep continuity where it helps and create isolated inboxes where it improves reliability.
